blocks.text: When you build an MCP tool, sooner or later something will go wrong inside it. A file will be missing, an API will time out, or an argument will be the wrong shape.
MCP gives you two very different ways to talk about failure, and mixing them up causes real confusion for both developers and the LLM using your tool.
In this topic we will look at the difference between a protocol level error and a tool level error, and how to write tool code that fails gracefully every time.
1. Two Kinds of Errors
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440587201-45801102.png
MCP has exactly two places where something can be reported as an error, and they mean very different things.
The first is the protocol level, where the request itself is malformed or the method does not exist.
The second is the tool level, where the request was perfectly valid but the tool ran into trouble while doing its job.

items: Protocol level error, something is wrong with the request or the connection itself
Tool level error, the request was fine, but the tool could not complete the work it was asked to do

blocks.text: 2. Protocol Level Errors, the JSON RPC Kind

blocks.alt: Protocol Level Errors, the JSON RPC Kind
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440587201-222037995.png
MCP is built on JSON RPC, and JSON RPC has its own standard error format.
A protocol level error means the server could not even understand or route the request properly.
Common causes include calling a method that does not exist, sending malformed JSON, or missing a required protocol field.

blocks.title: You rarely write these by hand
blocks.content: Protocol level errors are almost always generated by the MCP framework or transport layer itself, not by your tool code.

blocks.text: 3. Tool Level Errors, the isError Kind

blocks.alt: Tool Level Errors, the isError Kind
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440587201-857094277.png
A tool level error looks completely different, it is not a JSON RPC error at all.
It is a normal, successful response from the protocol point of view, just one where the tool is reporting that its own work failed.
The shape is a regular tool result, with a flag called isError set to true and a text block explaining what happened.

blocks.title: Same tool, two very different outcomes
blocks.content: A successful read and a failed read both return an ordinary tool result, only the isError flag and the text tell you which one happened.

blocks.text: 4. Why the Distinction Matters
The client and the LLM treat these two kinds of errors very differently, so mixing them up breaks things.
A protocol error usually means retrying the exact same call will never work, something structural is broken.
Nothing about the arguments the LLM chose caused a protocol error, so no amount of clever retrying on its side will fix it.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Protocol Level Error","Tool Level Error"],"rows":[["Where it happens","Before the tool even runs","Inside the tool own logic"],["How it looks","A JSON RPC error object","A normal result with isError true"],["Typical cause","Bad method name or malformed request","An exception raised while running the tool"],["Who can fix it next","The client or transport code","The LLM, by changing its next call"]]}

blocks.text: A tool level error, on the other hand, is often something the LLM can fix simply by trying again with better arguments.
5. What a Tool Should Never Do
The single worst thing a tool can do is let an unhandled exception crash the whole server process.
One bad file path or one flaky network call should never take down every other tool in the same server.

blocks.title: A crash is the worst outcome
blocks.content: If the server process dies, every tool in that session becomes unavailable, not just the one that failed. Always catch, never let it propagate to the top.

items: Letting an unhandled exception crash the whole server process
Returning a raw stack trace as the only explanation
Silently swallowing the error and returning an empty success result
Returning isError true with no text explaining what actually happened

blocks.text: 6. Catching Exceptions Inside a Tool
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440691863-885797151.png
The fix is simple in shape, wrap the risky part of your tool in a try block.
Every branch of the except clause should return a normal, well formed result, never let the exception keep travelling upward.
7. Turning an Exception Into a Clean isError Result

blocks.alt: Turning an Exception Into a Clean isError Result
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440691865-394074056.png
The same pattern works in any language, the shape of the try and catch stays the same.
Here is a JavaScript version that wraps a generic tool call and converts any thrown error into a clean isError result.
Notice that the catch block never re throws, it always returns a normal object the client can display.
8. Giving the LLM Enough Information to Retry

blocks.alt: Giving the LLM Enough Information to Retry
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440691865-103874399.png
An error message is not just for a human reading logs, it is often the only thing the LLM sees about what went wrong.
A vague message forces the LLM to guess, and guessing usually means repeating the exact same failing call.
A good message tells the LLM three things, what failed, why it failed, and what to try differently next time.

items: Say what was wrong, not just that something was wrong
Name the exact field, path, or value that caused the failure
Suggest a concrete next step the LLM can take
Keep it short, one or two clear sentences is usually enough

blocks.text: 9. Good vs Bad Tool Error Messages
Small wording changes make a huge difference in whether the LLM can recover on its own.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bad Message","Good Message"],"rows":[["Error","File not found at reports/march.csv, check the path and try again"],["Something went wrong","The API returned a rate limit response, wait a moment and retry with fewer items per request"],["Invalid input","The field age must be a positive integer, you sent negative five"],["Exception: NoneType object has no attribute strip","The user record was empty, check that the user id exists before calling this tool"]]}

blocks.text: Every good example names the exact problem and points toward a fix, the bad ones just announce that failure happened.
10. Structuring Error Details for Complex Failures
Sometimes one sentence is not quite enough, especially for tools with many possible fields or a large schema.
You can still keep the result simple, just make the single text block richer with the specifics the LLM needs.
Listing the valid options directly in the message turns a dead end into something the LLM can act on immediately.
11. Timeouts and External Service Failures
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440691865-817850314.png
Many tools call out to a database, an API, or another service, and any of those can be slow or unreachable.
These failures are different from a bad argument, the input was fine, the outside world just did not cooperate.

blocks.title: Timeouts deserve their own clear message
blocks.content: Tell the LLM whether it is safe to retry immediately, or whether it should wait a moment first. Do not just say request failed.

blocks.text: A short retry hint here saves several wasted round trips, since the LLM would otherwise just repeat the exact same call.
12. Validation Errors Before You Even Try
Not every error needs a try and catch around risky code, some problems are obvious before you do any real work.
Checking inputs up front and returning a clear isError result early is often cleaner than catching a deep exception later.

items: Check required fields are present before doing any real work
Check types and ranges match what the schema promised
Check the value makes sense for this specific tool, like a positive quantity
Return isError true immediately with a clear message if any check fails

blocks.text: 13. Logging Versus What the LLM Sees
Your server logs and the message you send back to the LLM should not be the same text.
Logs can be as detailed as you like, the message the LLM sees should be short, safe, and useful.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Goes to Your Logs","Goes to the LLM in isError"],"rows":[["Full stack trace","One clear sentence about what failed"],["Internal file paths and stack frames","The specific part of the input that was invalid"],["Database connection strings","A suggestion for what to change next"],["Internal request id for debugging","Nothing that leaks secrets or internal details"]]}

blocks.text: 14. Worked Example
Let us build a small calculator tool and walk through every place it can fail.
The tool supports add, subtract, multiply, and divide, and each failure mode gets its own clear message.
Notice that the unknown operation case is checked directly, no exception needed, while divide by zero and bad types are caught.
Every single path out of this function is a clean, well formed result, nothing here can ever crash the server.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Letting an unexpected exception crash the entire MCP server process
Returning a raw stack trace or exception string as the whole message
Using isError true with an empty or vague text block
Confusing isError with the protocol level JSON RPC error object
Logging secrets or internal paths into the message the LLM actually sees
Never testing what happens when a dependency like a database or API is down

blocks.text: 16. Practice
Try writing a small tool called fetch_weather that takes a city name as its only argument.
Work through the failure cases below and give each one a message the LLM could actually act on.

items: Raise an error path for an empty city string, and catch it with a message asking for a valid city name
Add a check for a city name that does not match any known place, suggesting the LLM double check the spelling
Add a check for when the weather service itself times out, telling the LLM it is safe to retry shortly

blocks.text: When you are done, read each message back as if you were the LLM, and ask whether it actually tells you what to change.
17. Key Takeaway
A protocol level error means the request itself was broken, a tool level isError means the request was fine but the work failed.
Catch every exception inside your tool, and turn it into a short, specific message that tells the LLM exactly what to change before it tries again.
